questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I knew I wanted to go abroad to a country very far away to challenge myself more and preferrably a place where English wasn't very used so I would have to learn how to talk to people in another language to do even simpler things. I had a growing interest in Korea and therefore felt a slight connection as I did know a bit about what to expect being in the country and meeting the culture and people and thereby would also havr a bigger chance of having something in common with other international students.
In my choosing I also thought about the general safety and access to the health care of a country, in which Korea ranked high.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: At first it was very confusing, especially as a graduate since a lot of the information I did get early on was directed at undergrad students. Finding the course list available for international grad students was hard for example. Covid 19 did make it more confusing as there was a lot more steps to every process but as we got closer to course add/drop they did end up giving out correct and detailed guides and information. We also got a welcome package/book as school began. This seemed kind of late as several of the steps in the guides had already past before we got it. Again Covid 19 kind of was to blame as well as there was no real introduction besides a short video, whereas normally you would all have met a korean buddy, gone to orientation etc. Which was all cancelled as we couldn't meet physically

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Even though I arrived pretty early and in a messy situation (having to quarantine by myself for 14 days) the university already connected with me on mail and had me contact them daily and answered most questions I had. The global service center has a super quick response whenever I had questions. I did get connected to a Korean buddy before school started as well but since we couldn't meet, this wasn't as helpful as I thought it would be. Besides this we also get offered to connect with a mentor, a korean student who can help with all academic things, and a æanguage exchange buddy who will teach you korean.
Most help from the school itself came through email and was ok, though a bit late with important informations making it a bit stressful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Had it not been during the pandemic, I'm sure it would have been a 5

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I was late in finding housing as I did apply for the dorms but not getting a spot (which I am now thankful for), meaning I actually went to Korea before having housing.
I used a mix of facebook groups and korean craigslist (which is apparently trustworthy in Korea)
After my quarantine I went for a visit at a suitable place to be sure it looked as pictured and then signed the lease the same day.

I ended up living in a large sharehouse with 12 other people in a house called Kongstay and would definitely reccomend. We lived 5 minutes from campus, had the ease of the metrostation and busstop nearby, while still living in a pretty quiet residential area. We had freedoms the dorms do not, but ofcourse also paid for it with around 700k won a month for rent and maintanence. Can be found cheaper further away. Would not reccomend goshiwons, as they are too cramped and noisy, one rooms and officetels can be reccomended if a sharehouse isn't your thing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus living is a lot more freedom. If ypu want the community of dorm living it's as simple as finding a sharehouse. It's pricier than the dorms but to me it was worth it for the freedom and house experiences I got.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
As a Grad student it is a lot easier than the undergrads as Grad course selection only has one round in which it went smooth and I got all the classes I wanted after changing one halfway through add and drop.
Undergrads have several rounds though and just seeing my friends go through that system and again and again not getting the courses they wanted was stressfull.
Final course selection is also very late which can seem a bit stressfull (basically as the first week of classes begin you are still trying to pick your courses)

For grads you basically just browse the course site to find english taught courses open for exchange students that you would like, write down the course codes and as add/drop opens you go in and add them with the codes. After the opening you have a few days to then change your courses by dropping the ones you don't want and hopefully being able to then add the one you want.
Undergrads will have two free passes (which are basically extra spots in any given course) to apply for courses directly through the teacher who can add them manually if they are okay with adding an extra spot in their class.

Grad students do not have these passes which did stress me out in the beginning, as relevant courses on grad level for me were kind of lacking. Thankfully I was able to still get added to a class after initial selection as I had to drop another course by simply talking to the professor directly through mail.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I used the global service center for questions relevant to course selection. Besides this we had also gotten a digital guide and a mail about the process from our buddies.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I ended up getting all the classes I wanted.
It does seem like it is a lot easier to get into courses on grad level as there a fewer students than undergrads who have to compete for spots.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Inform yourself - find all the information you can and have your preferred courses prepared before add/drop. Be quick and don't be scared to just contact a professor directly to ask for a spot. The professor are all very friendly.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took three graduate level courses all of which were in different departments and had different diffculties.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I took a contemporary art class which compared to my home studies in comparative literature was quite easy as it was mainly lecture based with one 3 hr lecture a week and very few but good readings. I also did have quite an easy time following along as I did take a contemporary art class during my undergrad studies as well and the amount of homework and classwork was very low as most knowledge was to be learned during lectures. Our midterm was also changed from a 40 minute test into a final report on the class and final exam instead which the professor let us decide as a democracy.

My film theory class used so many interesting teaching styles. Each week we watched a movie, read a theoretical relevant text and wrote a short blogpost sharing our views and thoughts and then had 3 hrs of lecture mixed with debates and discussions and a student presentation on the movie. The final exam and midterm was a free choice between research paper or creative project with report - which I really appreciated. In the final weeks we had a workshop where we just had creative fun with the knowledge we had gained and then the last week was a class conference where everyone presented their final project.

Lastly I took a history class in which the level felt really high. This was based on several readings a week and classes were based on 3 hrs paper presentation and discussions as each time a student was picked as discussion leader. We worked very long and focused on the final research and the teacher was very strict along the way but ended up being quite generous with her grades.

All courses were graded on different aspects as professors choose themselves what to weight when grading, I had a less stressfull time during midterm as one of mine was changed and the two other's were presentation based.

All courses final exams were oral based with film theories and gender history having a class conference where every student present their final to the other students, and a final paper, and my art course had a 45 minute oral presentation to the class with debate and questions after.

All in all I was quite surprised at the different levels of difficulty as it varied a lot.
I was also quite surprised that the oral parts of exams were all class based in front of all students. Which I was stressed about but actually ended up liking more than what I'm used to at home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: MAC638 Film Theories med Helen as professor, IMA614 Contemporary Art Theory with Raul as professor and HOK744 Study on the Political History in the Late 19th Century with Leighanne as professor.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would wholeheartedly reccommend any course you can find with Helen Sin (신 혜린) as she was by far the best teacher I have ever had in my life and her course Film theories the best course I've ever had. She created an amazing class environment for learning and I always felt excited to share my interpretations and knowledge in a way I've never felt like before. She supports and cares about all her students and their potential working for everyone to reach their full portential.

If interested in art and okay with 3 hour lectures I would also reccommend Raúl Sampaio Lopés course as I did learn a lot and didn't feel too burdened.

Lastly I'm not sure if I would reccommend Leighanne as a professor. Before going I saw her name mentioned positively by previous exchange students and therefore picked her class. The material and subject itself was very interesting (so interesting in fact that I decided to go further with it and do my final thesis on it) but as a teacher I did not enjoy having her at all. She was cold, rude, pressuring and unempathetic. Having her class brought on anxiety weekly as I feared her classes. You were never right and you never did well in her class.
The grade she gave did not reflect how she treated me throughout the semester which makes me think this way of being is just her particular teaching style.
Besides her personality I didn't particularly like the structure of the classes. Barely any lecturing and only discussions. I felt like she wanted me to know so much that she didn't even teach me since she rarely spoke. I'm sure she is super smart and knowledgable but besides picking texts for our classes and telling us when we were wrong she barely taught me anything.

Food DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
They just made it mandatory for long term residents to have national health insurance on top of your own insurance from home. Which felt like a ridiculous way to double spend.

Everything could be done cheaper than I did. I lived in a pretty expensive house, travelled around a lot and ate lunch and dinner/got coffee/dessert out mostly every day.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries. Which means I ended up mostly eating out as it was cheaper than buying and cooking for yourself.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: it's kind of hard to judge as most things were shut down during the pandemic

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I am unsure as most things were shut down for health reasons

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Again I don't feel like I can comment on that.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Travel around, do a few bigger trips and some smaller daytrips. Getting around is easy you just have to plan a little bit.

I would reccomend Busan, Jeju, Paju, Nami Island and all parts of Seoul :)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: For me it was quite easy but I was also pretty prepared and already knew about the culture

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Korean students - sign up for both mentor and language buddy - this will be your one way tickets to social interactions with local students.
By lucl you can get good courses with local students as well.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The friendliness
Everyone seemed very kind, helpful and nice

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't stress too much about your exams and grades ( they'll turn out just fine!), balance your time! Dont just focus on school, remember to go out and do what you want, time flies by so quickly

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not really

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made and the self confidence I gained

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out how much work I needed to put into my courses. And then prioritizing some free time

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
